about: Obertauern is a purpose-built winter sports resort on the Radstädter Tauern pass in Salzburger Land, split between the communities of Tweng and Untertauern. The village sits on the pass itself — the lifts leave from the main street in every direction.
The cameras on this page are pass cameras as much as ski cameras: they show the Tauern road and the slopes in a single frame.
obertauern.access: Obertauern stands on the Radstädter Tauern pass between Untertauern and Tweng, on the B99 over the Tauern range. The pass road is the resort — the cameras here watch the summit stretch and the descents on both sides.

about: Poiana Brașov is Romania's best-known ski resort, a neighbourhood of Brașov at about 1,020 metres above sea level. Modernization in the 2010s expanded its ski area from 50 to 80 hectares and its slopes from 13.8 km to 23.9 km, most now covered by snow cannons.
In 2013 it hosted alpine skiing, figure skating and short track at the European Youth Olympic Winter Festival. Cable cars climb to the Cristianu Mare and Postăvaru summits above the resort.
poiana-brasov.access: Poiana Brașov is 12 km by road from the city of Brașov, served by regular buses (lines 20 and 100) and resort minibuses from the hotels to the base. The cameras on this page cover the climb from Brașov and the resort bowl beneath Postăvaru.

about: Rukatunturi — Ruka — is a 492-metre fell and ski resort in Kuusamo, Finland, whose first slope, Eturinne, opened in 1954. Today 41 slopes run on 21 lifts, with snowmaking from some 90 snowguns covering nearly all runs.

Ruka hosts the FIS Nordic Combined World Cup season opener each year, and around it lie over 500 km of cross-country tracks and the southern end of the Karhunkierros trail. The cameras on this page cover the fell and the village at its foot.
ruka.access: Ruka stands in Kuusamo in Finland's northeast, near the Russian border country. The resort village sits at the fell's base — the cameras here watch the village, the front slopes and the Kuusamo road corridor.

about: The Rusutsu Resort is the largest resort in Hokkaido, Japan, operated by Kamori Kanko. Famous for its ski slopes, it also offers an amusement park and golf courses in summer — a full-scale resort complex on the Shiribetsu plain.
The cameras on this page cover Rusutsu's mountains and the corridor between Lake Toya and the Niseko range that serves it.
rusutsu.access: Rusutsu stands in the village of Rusutsu in Hokkaido's Shiribetsu subprefecture, on the corridor between Sapporo, Lake Toya and Niseko. The cameras here watch that highway and the resort's mountains above it.

about: Saalbach-Hinterglemm is a municipality in the Pinzgau district of Salzburg, Austria, well known for its skiing. Its four-piste network — Saalbach, Hinterglemm, Fieberbrunn and Leogang — adds up to 270 kilometres of slopes.
The resort is a short transfer from Salzburg Airport. The cameras on this page cover the Glemmtal valley, the twin villages and the circus of lifts above them.
saalbach-hinterglemm.access: Saalbach-Hinterglemm fills the Glemmtal valley in the Pinzgau, reached from Zell am See and Maishofen. The valley road threads both villages — the cameras here watch that road and the slopes closing the valley's head.

about: Sälen, in Dalarna County, Sweden, is best known as the start of Vasaloppet — the world's oldest (since 1922) and largest cross-country ski race, with over 15,000 participants in the main race. It is also a cluster of seven alpine ski resorts: the oldest, Högfjällshotellet, dates to 1937.

Newer areas like Hundfjället and Stöten bring the vertical to 350 m; SkiStar operates the linked Lindvallen–Högfjällshotellet and Tandådalen–Hundfjället pairs. The cameras on this page cover the Sälen fjälls and the village.
salen.access: Sälen is a locality in Malung-Sälen Municipality on the Västerdalälven river in western Dalarna. The drive climbs from Malung into the fjäll country — the cameras here watch the village and the string of ski areas along the valley.

about: Shiga Kogen is a ski resort and hiking area in the highlands of Yamanouchi, Nagano, inside Joshin'etsu-kogen National Park. In 1980 an area of 13,000 hectares around it was designated a UNESCO Man and the Biosphere Reserve.
The ski area spreads as a linked plateau of valleys and peaks above the onsen town of Yamanouchi. The cameras on this page sample the plateau and the mountain road that crosses it.
shiga-kogen.access: Shiga Kogen spreads across the highlands above Yamanouchi, reached by the mountain road that climbs from the onsen town past the snow monkeys of Jigokudani toward the Shibutoge pass. The cameras here watch that road and the resort's separate valleys.

about: Shymbulak — also Chimbulak — is the largest ski resort in Central Asia, near Almaty, Kazakhstan. It sits in the upper Medeu Valley in the Zailiisky Alatau range at 2,200 metres above sea level.

The resort area lies about 25 km south of Almaty's city centre in the Medeo district, climbing from the famous Medeu skating rink into the Trans-Ili Alatau. The cameras on this page cover the resort and the valley road from the city.
shymbulak.access: Shymbulak is reached from Almaty by the Medeu Valley road, about 25 km south of the city centre, past the Medeu rink to the resort base at 2,200 m — or by the gondola that climbs from Medeu. The cameras here watch the valley and the resort terraces.

about: The Remarkables range rises sharply from the southeastern shore of Lake Wakatipu, forming Queenstown's famous backdrop. The range's highest point, Single Cone, reaches 2,319 metres, and Lake Alta sits in a glacial cirque below the Double Cone peaks.
The Remarkables Skifield climbs the range's northern face — the cameras on this page cover the skifield, its access road switchbacks and the lake shore it towers over.
the-remarkables.access: The Remarkables Skifield is reached from Queenstown via the winding access road that climbs from the Frankton flats to the base area high on the range. The cameras here watch that climb and the Wakatipu shore below.

about: Vuokatti, part of the municipality of Sotkamo in Finland's Kainuu region, is home to more than 6,000 inhabitants and a national Olympic Training Center for cross-country skiing, biathlon and Nordic combined.

Its hills — the highest, Porttivaara, at 345 m — hold a ski resort, a sports academy and a skiing tunnel that makes cross-country skiing possible in all seasons. The cameras on this page cover the resort slopes and the lakes district around Sotkamo.
vuokatti.access: Vuokatti stands in Sotkamo in the Kainuu lake district of eastern Finland, with its own railway station on the hill range of the same name. The cameras here watch the village, the resort hill and the Kajaani road corridor.

about: Ylläs — Yllästunturi — is a 719-metre fell in the municipality of Kolari in Finnish Lapland, and the highest fell in Finland with ski lifts. It is Lapland's second-largest ski resort after Levi.

Two villages serve it: Äkäslompolo on the north side and Ylläsjärvi in the south, connected by an 11 km road around the fell. The area counts 61 ski slopes, 29 lifts and 330 km of cross-country tracks, 38 km of them lit.
yllas.access: Ylläs stands in Kolari municipality in western Lapland; the nearest railway station is Kolari, 37 km away. The cameras on this page cover the twin villages, the fell road between them and the slopes above both.

about: Zao Onsen is a famous hot-spring town on Mount Zao in Yamagata, in the northern part of Honshu. The ski area spreads over the mountain above the town, climbing the volcano's flanks from the onsen streets.
The pairing is the point: ski the volcano by day, soak in the sulphur springs by night. The cameras on this page cover the town and the slopes climbing from its roofline.
zao-onsen.access: Zao Onsen sits on Mount Zao above Yamagata city, reached by the mountain road that climbs from the city into the onsen town. The cameras here watch that climb and the resort streets at its top.

about: Courmayeur is a town in Italy's autonomous Aosta Valley, serving as one of the two bases on either side of Mont Blanc — Europe's highest mountain — with Chamonix on the French side. Its lifts climb toward the great south face of the massif.
The cameras on this page cover the town, the Val Veny and Val Ferret valleys that flank it, and the Mont Blanc corridor it guards.
courmayeur.access: Courmayeur stands at the Italian end of the Mont Blanc Tunnel corridor, at the head of the Aosta Valley. The valley road and the tunnel approach meet at the town — the cameras here watch that junction and the lifts rising from the town's edge.

about: Granite Peak Ski Resort operates in Rib Mountain State Park, south of Wausau, Wisconsin. It features 58 runs and four terrain parks, with a vertical drop of 700 feet — the fourth tallest ski area in the Midwest.

Skiing on Rib Mountain began in 1937, making it one of the first ski areas in North America — only Stowe (1934) and Sun Valley (1936) predate it in this telling. Since 2000 the area has expanded significantly, adding seven chairlifts and a new base village.
granite-peak.access: Granite Peak stands on Rib Mountain just south of Wausau, ten miles north-northeast of Central Wisconsin Airport. The cameras on this page cover the Wausau corridor and the state-park mountain that rises over the Wisconsin River valley.

about: Diamond Peak is the community-owned ski area above Incline Village on Lake Tahoe's north shore — owned by the Incline Village General Improvement District rather than a resort corporation, and run for the town as much as for visitors. Its 655 acres climb from 6,700 feet to a summit of 8,540 feet, a 1,840-foot vertical that ranks among the largest on the lake, and the upper-mountain runs look straight down the length of Tahoe — the Lakeview Quad is named for exactly that view.

The terrain mixes groomed cruisers with named glades and tree skiing, and the mountain stays comparatively uncrowded by Tahoe standards. The cameras on this page sit over the base, the lifts and the lake-facing runs; the much larger nearby grid watches the two highways that serve the resort.
diamond-peak.access: Diamond Peak is reached by Ski Way, climbing from Country Club Drive in Incline Village. State Route 28 runs the lakeshore below the resort, and the Mt. Rose Highway (SR-431) starts just east of the village and climbs over the Carson Range to Reno. The NDOT cameras in the nearby grid below cover both roads — the drive in from Reno over the pass, and the lake-level run along SR-28.

about: Grouse Mountain is Vancouver's city mountain: a compact North Shore ski area whose runs look straight down over North Vancouver, the harbour and the downtown skyline. Four chairlifts and a magic carpet serve 33 runs on 86 hectares, and the mountain is as much an evening hill as a day one — 14 of its runs are lit for night skiing, so the cameras here keep working long after dark.

The ski terrain sits high on the mountain, reached from the base by the Skyride aerial tram. The signature run, The Cut, drops through the lights with the whole city spread below it, and the summit cameras double as one of the best live weather windows over Metro Vancouver — fog banks, clearing storms and sunset over the inlet included.
grouse-mountain.access: Grouse Mountain stands at 6400 Nancy Greene Way in North Vancouver, at the top of Capilano Road — a short drive from downtown Vancouver over the Lions Gate Bridge, or up Highway 1 to the Capilano Road exit. The Skyride gondola climbs from the base parking area to the alpine station beside the runs; city buses serve the base.

about: Myoko Kogen is not a single resort but a cluster of ski areas around the foot of Mount Myoko in Niigata: the hot-spring town of Akakura with its twin areas Akakura Onsen and Akakura Kanko, wide-open Ikenotaira, steep little Seki Onsen, and Suginohara, whose 8.5 km top-to-bottom run is among the longest in Japan and falls 1,124 metres from the area's highest lift-served point at 1,855 metres.

Sea-of-Japan storms bury the area — around 13 metres of snow in a season — and the resorts share one of Japan's classic powder reputations while keeping a traditional onsen-town feel that the big purpose-built resorts never had. The cameras on this page and in the surrounding valley watch the resort streets, the lift bases and the snow piling up on both.
myoko-kogen.access: Myoko-Kogen Station, on the Kita-Shinano Line 44 minutes from Nagano, is the area's railhead; buses climb from the station to Akakura Onsen town and the resort bases, and a shuttle links the Akakura, Ikenotaira and Suginohara areas along the mountain's foot.

about: Tomamu is Hoshino Resorts' mountain in Shimukappu Village, in the middle of Hokkaido's inland powder belt — a place cold enough that temperatures below −30 °C are part of its identity, which is exactly what keeps its snow dry when coastal resorts turn heavy. One gondola and five chairlifts serve 29 courses across two linked peaks, Tomamu Mountain and Tower Mountain, on about 124 hectares.

The skiing mixes long groomed cruisers — the longest runs pass four kilometres — with tree runs and a registered experts-only powder zone. The twin hotel towers at the base make it a true resort village in a way few Japanese ski areas are. The cameras here watch the towers, the lift bases and the cold, clear mornings the powder belt is famous for.
tomamu.access: JR Tomamu Station sits below the resort on the Sekisho Line — roughly 70 minutes by limited-express train from New Chitose Airport, with resort buses meeting arrivals. By road, the expressway crosses central Hokkaido into Shimukappu Village.

about: Voss Resort is the ski area above the town of Voss in Vestland, between Bergen and the fjords — 24 slopes and 40 km of groomed runs served by 11 lifts, topped by Hangurstoppen at 964 metres. The Voss Gondol rises straight from beside the town's railway station to the summit station, which makes it one of the few European resorts you can step onto from a train platform.

The skiing runs from the gondola-served Hanguren face down to the family slopes at Bavallen, with floodlit evening skiing three nights a week. The cameras on this page watch the mountain and the town; the road cameras around Voss watch the Bergen corridor and the fjord-country approaches.
voss.access: Voss is about 99 km east of Bergen, reached by road and by the Bergen Railway to Voss Station — the gondola's lower station stands beside the platforms and climbs to Hangurstoppen in under nine minutes. The resort's second welcome centre is at Bavallen, a short drive from the town centre.

about: Alta sits at the head of Little Cottonwood Canyon, southeast of Salt Lake City, and is one of the oldest ski areas in the United States — its first lift turned in January 1939. It is also one of only three American resorts that prohibit snowboarding, and its skiing is famously steep and fall-line, spread across two drainages: Collins Gulch and Albion Basin.

The canyon wrings more than 540 inches of snow out of an average season, and Alta's reputation rests on what that snow covers — the Baldy chutes, the long pitches off the Collins and Wildcat lifts, and tree skiing that stays cold for days after a storm. The cameras on this page watch the base areas and the canyon road below them.
alta.access: State Route 210 climbs Little Cottonwood Canyon from Sandy, in the southeast corner of the Salt Lake Valley, straight to Alta's base areas. The road is crossed by dozens of avalanche paths and carries traction restrictions during storms — the road cameras on this page matter here.

about: Deer Valley spreads across six peaks above Park City and is one of only three American resorts that prohibit snowboarding. It hosted the freestyle moguls and aerials at the 2002 Winter Olympics and is in line to host freestyle events again at the 2034 Games.

The skiing is weighted toward immaculate intermediate cruising on Bald Mountain and Flagstaff Mountain, with the steepest lines in the Daly Chutes and Empire Canyon. The Mayflower expansion on the resort's eastern side has taken the skiable total to 4,300 acres, among the largest in Utah. The cameras on this page cover the Park City approaches and the resort's base areas.
deer-valley.access: Deer Valley is in Park City, about 36 miles east of Salt Lake City via Interstate 80 and State Route 224, with its base lodges along Deer Valley Drive in town.

about: Angel Fire sits in the Moreno Valley, the high southern loop of the Enchanted Circle, and opened in 1966 as a family mountain for northern New Mexico. Its 80 trails spread over 560 acres of forested slopes, with the summit above 10,600 feet.

The base sits at 8,600 feet, high enough to hold snow through the New Mexico spring, and the mountain looks east across the valley toward the Sangre de Cristo range. The cameras on this page watch the base area and the valley road through the resort.
angel-fire.access: U.S. Route 64 crosses the Moreno Valley through Angel Fire, about 28 miles east of Taos on the Enchanted Circle; Eagle Nest and Cimarron Canyon continue east on the same road.

about: Red River is a former mining town on the Enchanted Circle whose ski area rises directly from Main Street — the lifts start in town and climb the forested slopes of the canyon wall above it. The mountain is compact: 209 acres and 64 trails between a base at 8,750 feet and a summit over 10,300 feet.

The town keeps its mining-era main street and a deliberately unhurried pace, and the ski area matches it — a locals' and families' mountain rather than a destination resort. The cameras on this page watch the canyon road through town and the slopes above it.
red-river.access: State Road 38 climbs the Red River canyon from Questa to the town and ski area, forming the northern arc of the Enchanted Circle between Taos and Eagle Nest.

about: June Mountain is the quieter sister of Mammoth Mountain, set in the June Lake Loop in the Eastern Sierra. Its skiing spreads over two peaks — Rainbow Mountain and June Mountain itself — above the loop's chain of lakes, across 1,500 acres weighted toward families and intermediates.

The mountain averages around 250 inches of snow a season and tops out just over 10,000 feet; it has long been marketed as California's family mountain, a slower-paced alternative to its famous neighbour. The cameras on this page cover the loop road and the U.S. 395 corridor below.
june-mountain.access: State Route 158, the June Lake Loop, leaves U.S. 395 north of Mammoth Lakes, runs past June Lake village to the ski area, and rejoins 395 at the loop's north end.

about: Hoodoo occupies Hoodoo Butte, a forested volcanic cinder cone at the summit of Santiam Pass, and has been skiing since 1938 — one of Oregon's first ski areas. Its 806 acres face northeast off the cone, served by five lifts, with night skiing under lights on weekends.

From the top, the central Cascade volcanoes line the horizon: Three Fingered Jack, Mount Washington and the Three Sisters. The cameras on this page double as a Santiam Pass road check — this is the crossing central Oregon watches in a storm.
hoodoo.access: U.S. Route 20 passes the ski area at the summit of Santiam Pass, 20 miles west of Sisters and about 40 miles northwest of Bend; Salem and Eugene lie west down the Santiam River canyon.

about: Blue Mountain is Ontario's largest ski resort, spread along the Niagara Escarpment above the southern shore of Georgian Bay. Founded in 1941, it is the third-busiest ski resort in Canada, with a pedestrian village at its base and 43 trails cut into the escarpment face.

The vertical is modest at 220 metres, but the escarpment catches lake-effect snow off the bay, and a large share of the terrain is lit for night skiing. The cameras on this page watch the slopes and the Collingwood corridor below the escarpment.
blue-mountain-ontario.access: The resort sits just west of Collingwood, reached by Highway 26 along the Georgian Bay shore — roughly two hours northwest of Toronto.

about: Pyhä — Pyhätunturi — is a fell resort in Finnish Lapland, built on the Kultakero slopes at the edge of Pyhä-Luosto National Park. The first lift opened in 1964, and since 1987 the resort has been run by the same company as Ruka in Kuusamo. Its 15 slopes include Huttu-Ukko, the steepest maintained piste in Finland.

The fell was a sieidi — a sacred place — for the Sámi long before skiing, and the national park beside the resort protects deep gorges and some of Finland's oldest forest. The cameras on this page watch the resort centre and the fell road, as useful for the aurora season as for snow.
pyha.access: Pyhä is reached by road via Kemijärvi, about 57 kilometres away; Rovaniemi and its airport are roughly 130 kilometres southwest, with SkiBus coaches running to the resort in season.

about: Oppdal is Norway's largest ski centre by area: four mountains — Vangslia, Hovden, Stølen and Ådalen — linked by 18 lifts and 56 kilometres of pistes above the village. Hovden, the original slope, opened in 1952, and its steep black runs remain the connoisseurs' corner of the mountain.

The centre spreads wide rather than high — 715 metres of vertical across a broad plateau landscape where the Dovre mountains meet Trollheimen. The cameras on this page cover the slopes and the E6 corridor through the village.
oppdal.access: Oppdal village stands on the E6 highway and the Dovrebanen railway between Trondheim and Dombås; the main Vangslia base area is a few minutes from the village centre.
